  --title "feat(security): base image remediation — Remediation tab, tag candidates, Dockerfile rewrite" \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
Implements §3.2 security remediation: discovering a scan finding's fixable
base images, listing and caching candidate registry tags, and rewriting the
Dockerfile in place with a previewed diff.

- Read a vulnerability's minimum fixed version from Trivy output.
- Discover Dockerfile base images and pick tag candidates within the allowed
  move (`internal/remediation`).
- One paginated tag lister shared across the OCI and remediation code.
- Scan a candidate image directly from its registry, cache the result.
- New Remediation tab: choose a base image, preview the diff, write on
  request, byte-range Dockerfile rewrite that only touches what was shown.
- A commit-hash tag has no resolvable version, and the UI says so instead
  of guessing.

## Test plan
- [ ] CI: Lint and build, Test
EOF
)" 2>&1

# MCP: exposing the features added since §3.61

Status: batches 1 to 4 decided and implemented on `feat/mcp-forward-templates-status`. Baseline: 17 tools in `internal/mcp/tools.go`.

## Constraints that decide everything

Taken from `docs/architecture/mcp.md`; not repeated in each item.

- Nothing in `internal/mcp` touches the router's model (Rule 110). State held by
  the router is reached through `mcp.Dispatcher`, buffered reply channel of one.
- No credential leaves: the absence of a field, not a filter. A test walks the
  types.
- An action is registered only if it is the headless form of a declared key in
  `internal/ui/keymap` (`mcpActionKeys`), and its inverse is not removed.
- Every context-dependent answer says which context served it.
- Only `net_check` touches the network today. Any second one is declared as such.
- `mcp.expose` stays the only authorization.

    needs and stay the thing that measures the result. It could not, because of
    four omissions.

    carried Message, Status and CauseMetadata.EndLine all along; the Finding
    built from it kept StartLine and discarded the rest, so a caller knew where
    a faulty block began and not where it ended — enough to display, not enough
    to replace. They are now on scan.Finding and projected by scan_result:
    
    - EndLine, with Line, is the span of the faulted block
    - Message is this instance's wording ("Specify at least 1 USER command"),

est-ce que la remediation de dockerfile fonctionne aussi pour les images dhi.io qui garde le même tag mais sont constamment mise à jour

  Searched for 1 pattern, ran 3 shell commands

Non, pas pour ce cas. La remédiation ne sait pas traiter une image dhi.io qui garde le même tag tout en étant mise à jour.

- Candidats : Candidates() (internal/remediation/tags.go:115) ne propose que des tags strictement plus récents que le tag actuel (comparaison de version, même variante). Sur un tag flottant, il n'y a aucun tag plus récent à proposer. Le résultat est vide, avec la raison « no newer tag of the same variant exists on this line ».
- Digest : le digest est parsé dans Ref.Digest, mais il n'est jamais utilisé pour choisir ou proposer un candidat. Une référence épinglée par digest ou sur latest est refusée avec « the reference has no tag — it is pinned by digest or floats on latest ».
- Le scan de l'image actuelle : le scan de la ligne courante fonctionne (ScanRemoteImage), mais il est mis en cache par référence (cache.SetRemediationResult(ref, …)). Un tag flottant peut donc afficher des comptes de CVE périmés, alors que l'image du registre a changé depuis le dernier scan.

Ce qui manquerait pour ce cas : soit rescanner le tag actuel en ignorant le cache, soit résoudre le tag en digest et réécrire le Dockerfile avec image:tag@sha256:…. Le second choix est celui de Dependabot et Renovate. Je peux détailler la conception si tu veux.

13981	| **Kyverno** (`kyverno apply`, règles `mutate`) | oui, hors cluster | Rend la **ressource réécrite entière**, pas un patch : commentaires et mise en forme sont perdus, ce que `Rewrite` garantit justement de ne pas faire. Et manifestes Kubernetes uniquement |
13982	| **KICS** (Checkmarx) | oui — mais *AI-guided remediation* | C'est exactement la voie LLM, et hébergée |
13983	| **Checkov** | non en CLI open source | Les correctifs sont dans la plateforme |
13984	| **kube-linter**, **hadolint**, **tflint** | non | Diagnostic seul |
13985	
13986	Conclusion : **un LLM n'est nécessaire que pour le cas ouvert** — transformer
13987	une `Resolution` arbitraire en patch. Pour un catalogue borné, le déterministe
13988	suffit et existe.
13989	
13990	Ce qui ne veut pas dire que le cas ouvert est interdit, mais qu'il se place
13991	ailleurs : la règle du projet n'est pas « pas de LLM », elle est « mesuré,
13992	jamais inféré ». Un patch proposé par un LLM **et jugé par un re-scan** la
13993	respecte ; un patch proposé et pas re-mesuré ne la respecte pas, quelle que
13994	soit son origine. C'est ce que §3.2 a fait en re-scannant les candidats plutôt
13995	qu'en pariant sur eux, et c'est exactement ce que l'étage 2 permet — le LLM y
13996	est celui de l'agent appelant, pas un que DevDesk embarquerait.
13997	
13998	**Le piège de Semgrep, et il est structurel** : les règles Trivy (AVD) et les
13999	règles Semgrep sont **deux catalogues différents**, et la correspondance entre
14000	eux n'existe pas. Brancher Semgrep, ce n'est donc pas « corriger ce que Trivy a
14001	trouvé », c'est **ajouter un quatrième outil** — avec son `tool_source.go`, son
14002	mode conteneur, son cache, sa catégorie — dont les findings ne coïncideront pas
14003	avec ceux de l'onglet Misconfigurations. Deux comptes qui se contredisent à
14004	l'écran coûtent plus que ce que l'autofix rapporte.

14007

14009	écrit ici, et le serveur MCP donne à l'agent appelant de quoi traiter le
14010	reste.** Les deux ne visent pas le même utilisateur et ne partagent aucun

14012

14022	sans I/O, avec un test par règle sur un fichier d'exemple.

14024	Ce catalogue est **délibérément fini**. Il ne cherche pas à couvrir Trivy : il

14032	La boucle de vérification est branchée elle aussi —

4117	## Securing Containers in Kubernetes
4118	
4119	Kubernetes is a powerful container orchestration platform. Since Kubernetes 1.24, Docker Engine (dockershim) has been fully removed, and containerd is now the default runtime. Although Docker and containerd share OCI image standards, Kubernetes has its own multilayered security model. In this chapter, we focus on modern Kubernetes security best practices in 2025, with an emphasis on pod security, runtime hardening, and secret management.
4120	
4121	Kubernetes’ security consists of the following layers:
4122	
4123	- Image & supply chain security: Scan images for vulnerabilities (Trivy, Grype), sign and verify them with Sigstore/Cosign, and generate SBOMs (Syft/Grype).
4124	- Pod security: Apply Pod Security Admission, avoid privileged containers, enforce security contexts, network policies, and least privilege.
4125	- Kubernetes control plane security: Protect API server, etcd, and kubelet with RBAC, audit logs, TLS, and restricted API access.
4126	- Runtime security: Monitor live workloads using Falco, Cilium Tetragon, or other eBPF-based tools for anomalies and malicious behavior, and integrate alerts with SIEM systems.
4127	
4128	As we mentioned earlier, Falco is a powerful runtime security tool that can be used to monitor and detect security threats in Kubernetes. It uses the Linux kernel's extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) to monitor system calls and detect malicious activities. Falco can be used to detect security threats such as privilege escalation, file manipulation, and
4129	
4130	network attacks.
4131	
4132	Until now, we discussed image security. In this chapter, we will discuss pod security which is still close to the Docker security model. We will introduce Kubernetes security contexts, pod security standards, and pod security admission. The next chapter is dedicated to Kubernetes control plane security and runtime. Kubernetes runtime security and monitoring are discussed in the last chapter of this section.
4133	
4134	## 6.1 TL;DR
4135	
4136	- Pod Security Admission (PSA) replaces deprecated Pod Security Policies (PSP).
4137	- Use Kubernetes Security Contexts to enforce non-root users, seccomp, and SELinux/AppArmor profiles.
4138	- Sign container images with Cosign/Sigstore and generate SBOMs for supply chain integrity.
4139	- Manage secrets with Kubernetes Secrets, Sealed Secrets, or External Secrets Operator.
4140	- Apply NetworkPolicies for Zero Trust communication between pods.
4141	- Monitor runtime behavior using Falco or Cilium Tetragon.
4142	
4143	Before jumping into the details of Kubernetes security, let's first step a bit more into Linux access control.
4144	
4145	## 6.2 Linux Access Control, DAC, and MAC
4146	
4147	Linux access control is based on the principle of least privilege. This principle states that a process should only have the minimum privileges required to perform its tasks. This is important as it reduces the attack surface of the system and prevents unauthorized access to sensitive resources. Linux access control is implemented using Discretionary Access Control (DAC) and Mandatory Access Control (MAC) .
4148	
4149	## 6.2.1 Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
4150	
4151	DAC is the traditional access control model used in Linux. It is based on the concept of user and group ownership of files and directories.
4152	
4153	When doing a ls -l in a directory, you will see the following output:
4154	
4155	```
4156	0 -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 Mar 7 12:00 file.txt
4157	```
4158	
4159	The rw-r--r-- part is the file's permission. It's divided into three parts: the first part is for the owner, the second part is for the group, and the third part is for others. The r stands for read, the w stands for write, and the x stands for execute. The - means that the permission is not granted.
4160	
4161	Each part of the permission is a 3-bit number: rwx. One can use the chmod command to change the permission of a file or directory:
4162	
4163	```
4164	# chmod 777 file.txt
4165	```
4166	
4167	This command will give the owner, the group, and others full access to the file. Now let's check the permissions again:
4168	
4169	$ ls –l
4170	
4171	And the output is:
4172	
4173	```
4174	0 -rwxrwxrwx 1 root root 0 Mar 7 12:00 file.txt
4175	```
4176	
4177	The chmod command can also be used to give specific permissions to the owner, the group, and others:
4178	
4179	# chmod 644 file.txt
4180	
4181	This is all DAC, the discretionary part of the access control.
4182	
4183	## 6.2.2 Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
4184	
4185	MAC is a more advanced access control model used in Linux. It is based on the concept of security labels and policies and requires the use of a security module such as SELinux or AppArmor. MAC is used to enforce mandatory access control policies on processes and files.
4186	
4187	At the time of writing this book, Ubuntu uses AppArmor by default, which is a MAC implementation. By installing and enabling SELinux, files are labeled, and those labels can be accessed by running ls -Z in a directory:
4188	
4189	```
4190	0 -rw-r--r--. 1 root root unconfined_u:object_r:admin_home_t:s0 0 Mar 7 12:00 file.txt
4191	```
4192	
4193	The unconfined\_u:object\_r:admin\_home\_t:s0 part is the security context of the file. It consists of the user, the role, the type, and the level:
4194	
4195	- User: The user that the file is associated with. The user is used to define the privileges and access rights of the file. Here, the user is unconfined\_u, which is the default user for unconfined processes. An unconfined process is a process that is not confined by a security policy.
4196	- Role: The role that the file is associated with. The role is used to define the rolebased access control policies of the file. Here, the role is object\_r, which is the default role for objects. An object is a file or a directory.
4197	- Type: The type of the file. The type is used to define the type-based access control policies of the file. Here, the type is admin\_home\_t, which is the default type for administrative home directories.
4198	- Level: The level of the file. The level is used to define the sensitivity of the file. Here, the level is s0, which is the default level for unclassified files. Other options are s1 , s2, and so on. The highest level is s15 .
4199	
4200	The level can also be a range, such as s0:c123,c456. This means that the file is associated with the s0 level and has the c123 and c456 categories. The c123 and c456 categories are used to restrict the access of the file to certain processes.
4201	
4202	Another example is s1-s15:c0.c600 which means that the file is associated with the s1 to s15 levels and can access containers with the c0 to c600 categories.
4203	
4204	## 6.2.3 SELinux Architecture
4205	
4206	SELinux, which stands for Security-Enhanced Linux, is a Linux kernel security module that allows you to enforce mandatory access control policies on processes and files. The SELinux architecture consists of the following components:
4207	
4208	- Security server: The security server is the core of SELinux. It is responsible for enforcing the security policies defined in the security policy database. The security server is implemented as a set of kernel modules that are responsible for enforcing the security policies on processes and files.
4209	- Subject: A subject is a process or a user that is subject to the security policies defined in the security policy database. A subject is assigned a security context that defines its privileges and access rights.
4210	- Object manager: The object manager is responsible for managing the security contexts of files and directories. It is implemented as a set of kernel modules that are responsible for assigning security contexts to files and directories.
4211	- Access vector cache: The access vector cache is a cache of access control decisions made by the security server. It is used to speed up access control decisions and
4212	
4213	reduce the overhead of enforcing the security policies.
4214	
4215	When a process tries to access a file, the security server checks the access vector cache for an access control decision. If the access vector cache contains an access control decision for the process and the file, the security server uses the access control decision to grant or deny access to the file. If the access vector cache does not contain an access control decision for the process and the file, the security server consults the security policy database to make an access control decision.
4216	
4217	## 6.2.4 AppArmor Usage
4218	
4219	AppArmor, similar to SELinux, is a Linux kernel security module that allows you to enforce mandatory access control policies on processes and files. AppArmor is different from SELinux in that it uses profiles to define the access control policies of processes and files. An AppArmor profile is a set of rules that define the access control policies of a process or a file.
4220	
4221	AppArmor supports access control for the following resources, among others:
4222	
4223	- files,
4224	- network,
4225	- mount points,
4226	- pivot\_root
4227	- and Unix domain sockets.
4228	
4229	To get started with AppArmor, you need to install the AppArmor packages on your system. E.g. on Ubuntu, you need the following packages:
4230	
4231	```
4232	$ sudo apt install apparmor-easyprof apparmor-notify apparmor-utils certspotter
4233	```
4234	
4235	The package apparmor-easyprof is used to create AppArmor profiles for processes. The package apparmor-notify is used to notify the user about AppArmor events. The package apparmor-utils is used to manage AppArmor profiles. The package certspotter is used to monitor SSL certificates and is only installed here to be used in the following examples.
4236	
4237	First, let's configure the certspotter. Create a directory called .certspotter under your home, and create a watchlist there, which is a list of domain names you want to check for SSL certificates:
4238	
4239	```
4240	$ mkdir ~/.certspotter
4241	```
4242	
4243	```
4244	$ echo "google.com" > ~/.certspotter/watchlist To create an AppArmor profile, let's use the aa-easyprof command: $ aa-easyprof /usr/bin/certspotter Here is the generated profile: 1 ## vim:syntax=apparmor 2 ## AppArmor policy for certspotter 3 ## ###AUTHOR### 4 ## ###COPYRIGHT### 5 ## ###COMMENT### 6 7 ##include <tunables/global> 8 9 ## No template variables specified 10 11 "/usr/bin/certspotter" { 12 ##include <abstractions/base> 13 14 ## No abstractions specified 15 16 ## No policy groups specified 17 18 ## No read paths specified 19 20 ## No write paths specified 21 } As you can see, everything is commented out. So, it's basically an empty profile. Let's store the profile somewhere: $ aa-easyprof /usr/bin/certspotter > /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.certspotter Now, we need to load the profile: $ sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.certspotter
4245	```
4246	
4247	Now, the profile is loaded and enforced. Now, try to run the certspotter command and see if it's working.
4248	
4249	```
4250	$ certspotter
4251	```
4252	
4253	The output should be something like this:
4254	
4255	```
4256	1 certspotter: /home/testuser/.certspotter/watchlist: 2 open /home/testuser/.certspotter/watchlist permission denied
4257	```
4258	
4259	This is because the profile is empty and doesn't allow the certspotter command to access the required resources. We can edit the profile to allow the certspotter command to access the required resources.
4260	
4261	The denial is logged in the /var/log/syslog file, but you can use AppArmor notify package to review the denials:
4262	
4263	```
4264	$ aa-notify -s 1 -v
4265	```
4266	
4267	This command will show the denials in the previous 24 hours. The -s option is used to specify the number of days to show the denials for. The -v option is used to show the denials in verbose mode.
4268	
4269	Here is an example profile that allows the certspotter command to access the watchlist file:
4270	
4271	```
4272	1 ## vim:syntax=apparmor 2 ## AppArmor policy for certspotter 3 ## ###AUTHOR### 4 5 ##include <tunables/global> 6 7 /usr/bin/certspotter { 8 #include <abstractions/base> 9 /home/testuser/.certspotter/watchlist r, 10 }
4273	```
4274	
4275	You can edit the profile in the /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.certspotter file and then load the profile using the apparmor\_parser command. The r stands for read. It allows the certspotter command to read the watchlist file.
4276	
4277	So far we have looked into access control in Linux. As containerized applications are also Linux processes, we can employ these practices. Let's first look into Kubernetes' built-in security enforcement implementation before getting into using SELinux and AppArmor in the Kubernetes context.
4278	
4279	## 6.3 Kubernetes Security Contexts
4280	
4281	Kubernetes' security contexts are used to define security settings for pods and containers. They are used to enforce security policies on pods and containers. An example usage of security contexts for a pod is shown below:
4282	
4283	```
4284	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod 3 metadata: 4 name: nginx 5 spec: 6 securityContext: 7 runAsUser: 1000 8 runAsGroup: 3000 9 fsGroup: 2000 10 containers: 11 - name: nginx 12 image: nginx:stable 13 securityContext: 14 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false 15 runAsNonRoot: true 16 readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
4285	```
4286	
4287	Listing 6.1: Kubernetes Pod Security Context example
4288	
4289	Here, we define a security context for the pod. Here we can set the user and group IDs for the containers to override the default ID of 0 that is associated with the root user. We set the runAsUser to 1000, the runAsGroup to 3000, and the fsGroup to 2000. The runAsUser and runAsGroup fields are used to define the user ID and group ID that the container runs as. The fsGroup field is used to define the group ID that the container's file system is associated with. These fields are used to enforce the use of non-root users in pods and containers, as the entered IDs (1000, 2000, and 3000) are non-zero IDs.
4290	
4291	A second security context is defined for the container. We set the allowPrivilegeEscalation field to false. This field is used to prevent privilege escalation in the container. Privilege escalation is the act of gaining higher privileges than the ones initially granted to a process. It is a common attack vector used by attackers to gain unauthorized access to a system. By setting the allowPrivilegeEscalation field to false, we prevent privilege escalation in the container. If the flag is set to false, the child processes of the container can't get more privileges than their parent process.
4292	
4293	If the containers are running as privileged or if they have the CAP\_SYS\_ADMIN capability, then this flag is set to true. And yes, this means we have control over the capabilities each container has in the context of Kubernetes.
4294	
4295	## 6.3.1 Set Linux Capabilities
4296	
4297	We discussed Linux capabilities in earlier chapters. Linux capabilities are used to grant specific privileges to a process. To set Linux capabilities for a container, you can use the capabilities field in the security context. An example usage of the capabilities field is shown below:
4298	
4299	```
4300	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod 3 metadata: 4 name: nginx 5 spec: 6 containers: 7 - name: nginx 8 image: nginx 9 securityContext: 10 capabilities: 11 add: ["NET_ADMIN"]
4301	```
4302	
4303	Listing 6.2: Kubernetes Pod Security Context with Linux capabilities
4304	
4305	Here, we define a security context for the container. We set the capabilities field to NET\_ADMIN. This grants the container the NET\_ADMIN capability. The NET\_ADMIN capability allows the container to perform network-related administrative tasks such as configuring network interfaces and setting up network bridges.
4306	
4307	To remove a capability from a container, you can use the drop field in the capabilities field:
4308	
4309	```
4310	1 capabilities: 2 drop: ["NET_ADMIN"]
4311	```
4312	
4313	To remove all capabilities from a container, you can use the ALL field in the capabilities field:
4314	
4315	```
4316	1 capabilities: 2 drop: ["ALL"]
4317	```
4318	
4319	To remove all, except for one:
4320	
4321	```
4322	1 capabilities: 2 drop: ["ALL"] 3 add: ["NET_ADMIN"]
4323	```
4324	
4325	Denying a process certain Linux capabilities restricts them from performing certain system calls. But capabilities are not the only way to do it.
4326	
4327	## 6.3.2 Set the Seccomp Profile
4328	
4329	Seccomp is a Linux kernel feature that allows you to restrict the system calls that a process can make. Seccomp stands for secure computing mode. It is used to reduce the attack surface of a process by restricting the system calls it can make. To set the seccomp profile for a container, you can use the seccompProfile field in the security context. An example usage of the seccompProfile field is shown below:
4330	
4331	```
4332	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod 3 metadata: 4 name: nginx 5 spec: 6 containers: 7 - name: nginx 8 image: nginx 9 securityContext: 10 seccompProfile: 11 type: RuntimeDefault
4333	```
4334	
4335	Listing 6.3: Kubernetes Pod Security Context with Seccomp profile
4336	
4337	The seccompProfile field is used to define the seccomp profile for the container. The type field is used to define the type of the seccomp profile. The RuntimeDefault type is used to use the default seccomp profile for the container. To use a custom seccomp profile, you can use the Localhost type:
4338	
4339	```
4340	1 seccompProfile: 2 type: Localhost 3 localhostProfile: /path/to/seccomp/profile.json
4341	```
4342	
4343	The profile.json file is a JSON file that contains the seccomp profile for the container. This file should be present in every node in the cluster under the same path. An example seccomp profile is shown below:
4344	
4345	```
4346	1 { 2 "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW", 3 "architectures": [ 4 "SCMP_ARCH_X86_64" 5 ], 6 "syscalls": [ 7 { 8 "names": [ 9 "open", 10 "close", 11 "read", 12 "write" 13 ], 14 "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW" 15 }, 16 { 17 "names": [ 18 "execve" 19 ], 20 "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO" 21 } 22 ] 23 }
4347	```
4348	
4349	Listing 6.4: Kubernetes Seccomp Profile example
4350	
4351	This seccomp profile allows the container to make the open , close , read, and write system calls. It disallows the execve system call, which is used to execute a new program.
4352	
4353	As we are moving towards Linux security practices, the next thing we're going to discuss is Kubernetes support for Linux-native access control.
4354	
4355	## 6.3.3 Set the SELinux Context
4356	
4357	SELinux, as explained before, is a Linux kernel security module that allows you to enforce mandatory access control policies on processes and files. To set the SELinux context for a container, you can use the seLinuxOptions field in the security context. An example usage of the seLinuxOptions field is shown as follows:
4358	
4359	```
4360	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod 3 metadata: 4 name: nginx 5 spec: 6 containers: 7 - name: nginx 8 image: nginx 9 securityContext: 10 seLinuxOptions: 11 level: s0:c123,c456
4361	```
4362	
4363	Listing 6.5: Kubernetes Pod Security Context with SELinux context
4364	
4365	Here, the level is set to s0:c123,c456 which is the last part of the MAC security context that we discussed earlier. To set a full SELinux context, you can use the user , role , type , and level fields:
4366	
4367	```
4368	1 seLinuxOptions: 2 user: system_u 3 role: system_r 4 type: container_t 5 level: s0:c123,c456
4369	```
4370	
4371	One can access an explanation about the different fields of the SELinux options by entering the following command on a Kubernetes cluster:
4372	
4373	```
4374	$ kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.securityContext.seLinuxOptions
4375	```
4376	
4377	It's important to keep this command handy, as Kubernetes security is young and subject to change.
4378	
4379	As SELinux has a minimalistic configuration, you can enforce a more complex access control with AppArmor, as discussed before.
4380	
4381	## 6.3.4 Set the AppArmor Profile
4382	
4383	Adding an AppArmor profile to a pod is done using metadata annotations. Here is an example:
4384	
4385	```
4386	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod 3 metadata: 4 name: nginx 5 annotations: 6 container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/nginx: runtime/default Listing 6.6: Kubernetes Pod Security Context with AppArmor profile
4387	```
4388	
4389	To use a custom AppArmor profile, you can use the localhost profile:
4390	
4391	```
4392	1 container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/nginx: 2
4393	```
4394	
4395	```
4396	localhost/path/to/apparmor/profile
4397	```
4398	
4399	Kubernetes supports different security enforcement implementations, but configuring each one separately is rather tedious and time-consuming. That's why Kubernetes offers bundled presets of them to provide security without much headache.
4400	
4401	## 6.4 Pod Security Standards
4402	
4403	Pod Security Standards defines three levels of security for pods: privileged , baseline, and restricted. These levels cover a wide range of security requirements for pods. The three profiles are defined as follows:
4404	
4405	- Privileged: This is the least secure profile. It allows the pod to run as privileged and use host namespaces. A privileged container has access to all the capabilities of the host machine, as well as access to all the devices. It is important to note that
4406	
4407	- privileged containers are not recommended for production use as they can lead to security vulnerabilities.
4408	- Baseline: This is the default profile. It does not allow the pod to run as privileged and use host namespaces. It is the recommended profile for most workloads and is restricted enough to prevent known privilege escalations.
4409	- Restricted: This is the most secure profile. It enforces the use of non-root users in pods and restricts the use of host namespaces. It is recommended for workloads that require a high level of security.
4410	
4411	The privileged profile is basically “everything is allowed”.
4412	
4413	Before we go further into details, let's take a look at different types of containers that we will see in the coming section:
4414	
4415	- Containers: Normal containers are the ones that contain your application.
4416	- Init containers: These are containers running for a purpose (as the name suggests, initialization). After they exit, the normal containers start. Init containers can be used to prepare the database, or any other state, before the application containers start.
4417	- Ephemeral containers: These containers are usually used temporarily for purposes like debugging. In the case a container is buggy, and we can't access it through normal means like kubectl exec, one can use kubectl debug command to spawn an ephemeral container and start digging into the issue.
4418	
4419	All the configurations discussed in the coming section can be checked with kubectl explain for possible changes or further development, for example:
4420	
4421	$ kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.securityContext.capabilities
4422	
4423	Okay, let’s investigate different profiles and their meanings now.

4426	
4427	Here, we will mention different security contexts that are enforced in the baseline profile. To get a full list of them please confer the official documentation.
4428

4430	- – spec.containers[*].securityContext.privileged
4431	- – spec.initContainers[*].securityContext.privileged

4433	- – spec.ephemeralContainers[*].securityContext.privileged

4435	- – spec.hostIPC: The host IPC namespace is used to isolate inter-process communication between processes. It is used to prevent processes from accessing each other's memory and resources. By disallowing the use of the host IPC namespace, we prevent processes from accessing each other's memory and resources.
4436	- – spec.hostNetwork: The host network namespace is used to isolate network resources such as network interfaces and IP addresses.

4498	## 6.4.2 Restricted profile
4499	
4500	The restricted profile is the most secure profile. It contains everything from the baseline profile and adds further restrictions:
4501	
4502	- Run as non-root: The following fields are restricted to accept only true as a value:
4503	- – spec.containers[*].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
4504	- – spec.initContainers[*].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
4505	- – spec.ephemeralContainers[*].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
4506	- Seccomp: The aforementioned seccomp fields have to be set to Localhost or
4507	- RuntimeDefault values and cannot be undefined or empty.
4508	- Capabilities: Containers must drop ALL capabilities and can only add back the NET\_BIND\_SERVICE capability.
4509	- Read-only root filesystem:
4510	- spec.containers[*].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem (and the same
4511	- fields for init/ephemeral containers) must be true or undefined; it cannot be set to false .
4512	- PrivilegeEscalation: The following fields are restricted to accept only false:
4513	- – spec.containers[*].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
4514	- – spec.initContainers[*].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
4515	- – spec.ephemeralContainers[*].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
4516	- Volume types: The spec.volumes[*] is restricted to accept only the following
4517	- types:
4518	
4519	- – spec.volumes[*].configMap: This type is used to define a ConfigMap volume. ConfigMaps are Kubernetes resources that allow you to store configuration data in key-value pairs.
4520	- – spec.volumes[*].csi: This type is used to define a Container Storage Interface (CSI) volume. CSI is a standard for exposing storage systems to containerized workloads.
4521	- – spec.volumes[*].downwardAPI: This type is used to define a Downward API volume. The Downward API is a Kubernetes feature that allows you to expose pod and container metadata to containers.
4522	- – spec.volumes[*].emptyDir: This type is used to define an empty directory volume. An empty directory volume is a temporary directory that is created when a pod is created and is deleted when the pod is deleted.
4523	- – spec.volumes[*].ephemeral: This type is used to define an ephemeral volume. An ephemeral volume is a volume that is created and deleted with the pod. It's different from an emptyDir volume in that it's not shared between containers in the pod.
4524	- – spec.volumes[*].persistentVolumeClaim: This type is used to define a Persistent Volume Claim (PVC) volume. A PVC volume is a volume that is backed by a Persistent Volume (PV) and is used to store data persistently across pod restarts.
4525	- – spec.volumes[*].projected: This type is used to define a Projected volume. A Projected volume is a volume that contains multiple sources of data such as ConfigMaps, Secrets, and downwardAPI.
4526	- – spec.volumes[*].secret: This type is used to define a Secret volume. A Secret volume is a volume that is used to store sensitive data such as passwords and keys. Secrets are Kubernetes resources that allow you to store sensitive data in key-value pairs.
4527	
4528	Now let’s talk about how to enforce these standards to the pods.
4529	
4530	## 6.5 Pod Security Admission
4531	
4532	Pod Security Admission (PSA) is a built‑in feature of Kubernetes (GA since v1.25) that enforces Pod Security Standards on pods. It offers a built-in admission controller, meaning that every request to the Kubernetes API server is checked against the PSA rules. If a request violates the PSA rules, it is rejected and not persisted in the cluster.
4533	
4534	There are three actions that can be performed automatically upon a violation of the PSA rules:
4535	
4536	- Enforce: The request is rejected and not persisted in the cluster.
4537	- Audit: The request is allowed and persisted in the cluster, but an audit event is generated. The audit event contains information about the request and the violation of the PSA rules and is recorded in the audit log.
4538	- Warn: The request is allowed and persisted in the cluster, but a user-facing warning is generated.
4539	
4540	These actions are called "modes". A namespace can configure any or all of these modes. It's all handled by the labels. A label for configuring PSA is of the following format:
4541	
4542	```
4543	1 pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>: <LEVEL>
4544	```
4545	
4546	Here, <MODE> can be enforce , audit, or warn . <LEVEL> can be privileged , baseline, or restricted. An example namespace configuration is shown as follows:
4547	
4548	```
4549	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Namespace 3 metadata: 4 name: default 5 labels: 6 pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline 7 pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
4550	```
4551	
4552	Listing 6.7: Kubernetes namespace with Pod Security Admission configuration
4553	
4554	Here, the default namespace is configured to enforce the baseline profile and audit the restricted profile.
4555	
4556	Let's see the Pod Security Admission in action. We're going to label the default namespace manually to see if we can then deploy a privileged container in it:
4557	
4558	```
4559	$ kubectl label ns default pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
4560	```
4561	
4562	This command will label the default namespace with restricted enforcement. Now let's create a manifest for a privileged pod:
4563	
4564	```
4565	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod
4566	```
4567	
4568	```
4569	3 metadata: 4 name: privileged-pod 5 spec: 6 containers: 7 - name: privileged-container 8 image: busybox 9 command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"] 10 securityContext: 11 privileged: true
4570	```
4571	
4572	Listing 6.8: Kubernetes Pod with privileged container
4573	
4574	Now, let’s try to deploy this pod:
4575	
4576	```
4577	$ kubectl apply -f privileged-pod.yaml
4578	```
4579	
4580	The command will return an error message, stating that it's forbidden to run a container in privileged mode.
4581	
4582	We should also mention that enforcement of network policies depends on the Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin deployed on the cluster. Calico and Cilium are among popular CNI plugins for Kubernetes. Some of the CNI plugins might support certain rules or not.
4583	
4584	PSA is a new way of enforcing security to a Kubernetes cluster. It replaced another system called Pod Security Policies.
4585	
4586	## 6.5.1 Pod Security Policies (Removed)
4587	
4588	Pod Security Policies (PSPs) were deprecated in Kubernetes 1.21 and fully removed in 1.25. They are mentioned here for historical context only. Use Pod Security Admission (PSA) instead, as shown in the previous section.
4589	
4590	## 6.6 Secrets Management
4591	
4592	Secrets are sensitive pieces of information such as passwords, keys, and tokens. They are used to authenticate and authorize access to resources. In Kubernetes, a secret is an object that contains a small amount of sensitive data such as a password or a token. Secrets are stored in the cluster and are used by pods.
4593	
4594	Avoid committing secrets—even Base64 encoded—to Git repositories. Base64 is just encoding, not encryption.
4595	
4596	For GitOps workflows, consider using Sealed Secrets or External Secrets Operator (ESO) instead of storing raw Kubernetes Secrets in Git.
4597	
4598	In the coming sections, we'll discuss how to create and manage secrets with Kubernetes and third-party services.
4599	
4600	## 6.6.1 Create a Secret
4601	
4602	To create a secret, you can use the kubectl create secret command. An example usage of the kubectl create secret command is shown below:
4603	
4604	```
4605	$ kubectl create secret generic my-secret --from-literal=password=REDACTED
4606	```
4607	
4608	To check the secret, you can use the kubectl get secret command:
4609	
4610	$ kubectl get secret my-secret -o yaml
4611	
4612	The output should be something like this:
4613	
4614	```
4615	1 apiVersion: v1 2 data: 3 password: MTIzNDU= 4 kind: Secret 5 metadata: 6 creationTimestamp: "2024-03-07T12:00:00Z" 7 name: my-secret 8 namespace: default 9 resourceVersion: "REDACTED" 10 uid: REDACTED-REDACTED-REDACTED-REDACTED 11 type: Opaque
4616	```
4617	
4618	Listing 6.9: Kubernetes Secret example
4619	
4620	Here, the password field is the secret data. It is base64 encoded. To decode the secret data, you can use the base64 command:
4621	
4622	```
4623	$ echo MTIzNDU= | base64 --decode
4624	```
4625	
4626	Or to get the password directly:
4627	
4628	- $ kubectl get secret my-secret -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -decode
4629	
4630	Now we need to make this secret available to the pods.
4631	
4632	## 6.6.2 Use a Secret in a Pod
4633	
4634	To use a secret in a pod, you can define the secret in the pod's spec. There are two ways for doing this, based on how you want to make the secret available:
4635	
4636	- Mount a volume making the secret available as a file,
4637	- Expose the secret as an environment variable.
4638	
4639	Mounting a volume is safer, introducing an environment variable is more convenient. Here is an example for mounting the secret into the container:
4640	
4641	```
4642	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod 3 metadata: 4 name: my-pod 5 spec: 6 containers: 7 - name: my-container 8 image: my-image 9 volumeMounts: 10 - name: secret-volume 11 mountPath: /etc/secrets 12 volumes: 13 - name: secret-volume 14 secret: 15 secretName: my-secret
4643	```
4644	
4645	Listing 6.10: Kubernetes Pod with Secret volume mount
4646	
4647	An example usage of a secret in a pod as an environment variable is shown below:
4648	
4649	```
4650	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod 3 metadata: 4 name: my-pod
4651	```
4652	
4653	```
4654	5 spec: 6 containers: 7 - name: my-container 8 image: my-image 9 env: 10 - name: MY_PASSWORD 11 valueFrom: 12 secretKeyRef: 13 name: my-secret 14 key: password
4655	```
4656	
4657	Listing 6.11: Kubernetes Pod with Secret as environment variable
4658	
4659	This way, the MY\_PASSWORD environment variable is set to the value of the password key in the my-secret secret. To check the environment variable, you can use the kubectl exec command:
4660	
4661	```
4662	$ kubectl exec my-pod -- env
4663	```
4664	
4665	The output should be something like this:
4666	
4667	```
4668	0 MY_PASSWORD=REDACTED
4669	```
4670	
4671	As Kubernetes has means to store secrets, one can also import secrets from third-party services into the cluster.
4672	
4673	## 6.6.3 Populate a Secret from a third-party service
4674	
4675	It's not a good practice to save your secrets in your Kubernetes manifest files, as they will stick in your git history and can be exposed. Instead, you can use a third-party service to store your secrets and populate your Kubernetes secrets from there. One can for example use the aws-secrets-manager-csi-driver to populate secrets from AWS Secrets Manager. The AWS Secrets Manager CSI Driver is a Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver that allows you to use AWS Secrets Manager to store and manage secrets for your Kubernetes workloads.
4676	
4677	To use the AWS Secrets Manager CSI Driver, you need to install the driver on your cluster. You can use the following command to install the driver:
4678	
4679	```
4680	$ helm repo add secrets-store-csi-driver \
4681	```
4682	
4683	```
4684	https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/secrets-store-csi-driver/charts $ helm install -n kube-system \ csi-secrets-store secrets-store-csi-driver/secrets-store-csi-driver
4685	```
4686	
4687	These commands add the secrets-store-csi-driver Helm repository and install the secrets-store-csi-driver chart in the kube-system namespace.
4688	
4689	After installing the driver, you can create the following Kubernetes resources to use the driver and populate your secrets from AWS Secrets Manager:
4690	
4691	```
4692	10
4693	```
4694	
4695	```
4696	1 apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1 2 kind: SecretProviderClass 3 metadata: 4 name: aws-secrets-manager 5 spec: 6 provider: aws 7 parameters: 8 objects: | 9 - objectName: my-secret objectType: secretsmanager
4697	```
4698	
4699	Listing 6.12: Kubernetes SecretProviderClass for AWS Secrets Manager
4700	
4701	Here, we define a SecretProviderClass resource that uses the aws provider and populates the my-secret secret from AWS Secrets Manager. The objects field is used to define the objects that are populated from AWS Secrets Manager. To use an AWS Secrets Manager provider, you need to create a secret in AWS Secrets Manager and grant the necessary permissions to the driver to access the secret.
4702	
4703	After creating the SecretProviderClass resource, you can access the populated secret in your pods using the following Kubernetes resources:
4704	
4705	```
4706	1 apiVersion: v1 2 kind: Pod 3 metadata: 4 name: my-pod 5 spec: 6 containers: 7 - name: my-container 8 image: my-image
4707	```
4708	
4709	```
4710	9 volumeMounts: 10 - name: secret-volume 11 mountPath: /etc/secrets 12 volumes: 13 - name: secret-volume 14 csi: 15 driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io 16 readOnly: true 17 volumeAttributes: 18 secretProviderClass: "aws-secrets-manager"
4711	```
4712	
4713	Listing 6.13: Kubernetes Pod with AWS Secrets Manager CSI Driver
4714	
4715	Here, we define a pod that mounts the my-secret secret from AWS Secrets Manager to the /etc/secrets directory. The csi field is used to define the CSI driver that is used to mount the secret. The secretProviderClass field is used to define the SecretProviderClass resource that is used to populate the secret from AWS Secrets Manager.
4716	
4717	To expose the secret as an environment variable, you can use the env field in the pod's spec:
4718	
4719	```
4720	1 # SecretProviderClass update (add secretObjects) 2 apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1 3 kind: SecretProviderClass 4 metadata: 5 name: aws-secrets-manager 6 spec: 7 provider: aws 8 parameters: 9 objects: | 10 - objectName: my-secret 11 objectType: secretsmanager 12 secretObjects: 13 - secretName: aws-secret-synced 14 type: Opaque 15 data: 16 - objectName: my-secret 17 key: password 18 ---
4721	```
4722	
4723	```
4724	19 # Pod consuming the synced Secret 20 apiVersion: v1 21 kind: Pod 22 metadata: 23 name: my-pod 24 spec: 25 containers: 26 - name: my-container 27 image: my-image 28 env: 29 - name: MY_PASSWORD 30 valueFrom: 31 secretKeyRef: 32 name: aws-secret-synced 33 key: password 34 volumeMounts: 35 - name: secret-volume 36 mountPath: /etc/secrets 37 volumes: 38 - name: secret-volume 39 csi: 40 driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io 41 readOnly: true 42 volumeAttributes: 43 secretProviderClass: "aws-secrets-manager"
4725	```
4726	
4727	Listing 6.14: Kubernetes Pod with AWS Secrets Manager CSI Driver and Secret as environment variable
4728	
4729	Here, the secret is loaded from the secret-volume volume and exposed as the MY\_PASSWORD environment variable.
4730	
4731	## 6.7 Network Policies
4732	
4733	Network Policies are used to define the network access rules for pods. They are used to control the traffic that is allowed to and from pods. Network Policies are implemented using the NetworkPolicy resource in Kubernetes. An example usage of a NetworkPolicy
4734	
4735	resource is shown below:
4736	
4737	```
4738	1 apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 2 kind: NetworkPolicy 3 metadata: 4 name: my-network-policy 5 spec: 6 podSelector: 7 matchLabels: 8 app: my-app 9 policyTypes: 10 - Ingress 11 - Egress 12 ingress: 13 - from: 14 - podSelector: 15 matchLabels: 16 app: my-other-app 17 ports: 18 - protocol: TCP 19 port: 80 20 egress: 21 - to: 22 - podSelector: 23 matchLabels: 24 app: my-other-app 25 ports: 26 - protocol: TCP 27 port: 80
4739	```
4740	
4741	Listing 6.15: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy example
4742	
4743	Here, we define a NetworkPolicy resource that allows traffic to and from pods labeled with app: my-app. There are two main sections in the NetworkPolicy resource: ingress and egress .
4744	
4745	- Ingress: In Kubernetes Network Policies, the "ingress" refers to the incoming traffic to pods. It defines the rules that control which traffic is allowed to reach the pods.
4746	
4747	- Egress: In Network Policies, "egress" defines the rules that govern which traffic can leave the pods. It specifies the destinations to which the pods can send outbound traffic, controlling connections that pods can initiate.
4748	
4749	Another example would be a “deny all” policy, disallowing any traffic between the pods:
4750	
4751	```
4752	1 apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 2 kind: NetworkPolicy 3 metadata: 4 name: deny-all 5 namespace: default 6 spec: 7 podSelector: {} # This selects all pods in the namespace 8 policyTypes: 9 - Ingress # Deny all incoming traffic 10 - Egress # Deny all outgoing traffic
4753	```
4754	
4755	Listing 6.16: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy deny all example
4756	
4757	So, the absence of any ingress or egress rules in a NetworkPolicy means that all traffic is denied by default.
4758	
4759	Having a strict network policy is important for security reasons. When a pod is compromised, it can be used to attack other pods in the cluster. By using network policies, you can restrict the traffic that is allowed to and from pods and prevent unauthorized access to the cluster.
4760	
4761	For advanced scenarios, consider Cilium for L3/L4/L7-aware network policies and Kyverno for policy-as-code enforcement.
4762	
4763	## 6.8 Conclusion
4764	
4765	In this chapter, we discussed the security features of Kubernetes. We discussed the security contexts, Pod Security Standards, Pod Security Admission, Secrets Management, and Network Policies. We also discussed the security features of Linux such as DAC, MAC, and AppArmor. We also discussed the security features of SELinux.
4766	
4767	It's important to note that security is a complex topic and requires a deep understanding of the underlying technologies. As Kubernetes is still a relatively new technology, the security features are still evolving and improving. A good example is the deprecation
4768	
4769	of Pod Security Policies in favor of Pod Security Admission. It's important to stay up to date with the latest security features and best practices to ensure the security of your Kubernetes clusters.
4770	
4771	## 6.9 Exercises

4774	2. Create a network policy in your Kubernetes cluster and test it by creating pods and trying to access them from other pods.

14063	classe la plus nombreuse et celle où `Rewrite` par span ne suffit plus : la
14064	correction y est souvent *ajouter une clé dans un mapping*, ce qui demande un

### 3.79 La remédiation d'image de base ne sait rien faire d'un tag qui flotte (dhi.io, `:latest`) — **à faire**

§3.2 corrige une CVE d'image de base en proposant un tag **strictement plus
récent** du même repository. La question posée en session : est-ce que ça
fonctionne pour une image comme celles de [Docker Hardened
Images](https://www.docker.com/products/hardened-images/) (`dhi.io`), qui
gardent le **même tag** tout en étant reconstruites et republiées en continu ?
Vérifié dans le code, pas supposé : non.

**Trois endroits, trois raisons différentes.**

| Endroit | Ce qui se passe |
|---|---|
| `Candidates()` (`internal/remediation/tags.go:115`) | Ne compare que des versions strictement supérieures, même variante (`SplitTag`, ligne 93). Un tag flottant (`latest`, `latest-dev`, ou tout tag `dhi.io` sans numéro de version parsable) fait échouer `SplitTag` — retour `"the tag carries no version to move from"` |
| Le digest | `Ref.Digest` est parsé (`tags.go:43`) mais **jamais lu** pour choisir ou proposer un candidat. Une référence épinglée par digest est refusée telle quelle — `"the reference has no tag — it is pinned by digest or floats on latest"` (`tags.go:117`) |
| Le cache de scan | `cache.SetRemediationResult(ref, entry)` (`internal/ui/security/remediation_commands.go:129`) indexe par la référence **telle qu'écrite**. Sur un tag flottant, la référence ne change jamais — le compte de CVE affiché peut dater d'une image que le registre a déjà remplacée, et rien ne l'invalide |

Le résultat visible pour l'utilisateur : `ctrl+s` sur une base `dhi.io` (ou
toute base en `:latest`) répond « aucun candidat » — vide, pas faux, mais
silencieux sur la vraie raison, qui est que le mécanisme entier suppose une
version dans le tag.

**Ce que font Dependabot et Renovate pour ce cas exact** — vérifié le
2026-09-21 : les deux résolvent le tag flottant en son digest courant et
réécrivent la référence en `image:tag@sha256:…`. Ce n'est plus un choix
*parmi plusieurs candidats* — il n'y en a qu'un, le contenu actuel du tag — et
la mise à jour suivante attend que le digest change à nouveau. C'est une
opération différente de celle que §3.2 fait aujourd'hui : épingler, pas
choisir une version.

**Deux décisions restent ouvertes, volontairement pas prises ici :**

1. Comment détecter qu'un tag flotte. `SplitTag` renvoyant `""` (pas de
   version) est un signal mais pas une preuve — un tag versionné peut aussi
   être republié (rare, mais `latest-3.20` existe). Une liste de registres
   connus pour flotter (`dhi.io`, et tout `:latest`/`:main`/`:edge`) serait
   plus sûre mais demande une liste à tenir à jour.
2. Ce que DevDesk écrit une fois la détection faite. Deux réponses de forme
   très différente : (a) un simple re-scan qui ignore le cache — purement
   informatif, rien à réécrire, l'image est déjà « à jour » par construction
   — ou (b) réécrire le Dockerfile en `image:tag@sha256:…`, ce qui **fige**
   un tag qui était délibérément flottant. (b) change le contrat de l'image de
   base (elle cesse de suivre les correctifs amont sans intervention) et
   ressemble moins à une remédiation §3.2 qu'à une fonctionnalité voisine —
   l'épinglage par digest, que Dependabot et Renovate traitent d'ailleurs
   comme une politique séparée de la mise à jour de version.

Ni l'un ni l'autre n'est tranché ici : le catalogue actuel est correct sur ce
qu'il couvre (tags versionnés, même ligne ou major suivant), et ce cas est un
second mécanisme, pas un correctif du premier.

Sources vérifiées le 2026-09-21 :
[Docker Hardened Images](https://www.docker.com/products/hardened-images/),
[Dependabot — Docker ecosystem, digest pinning](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/dependabot/ecosystems-supported/supported-ecosystems-and-repositories#docker),
[Renovate — Docker datasource, digest pinning](https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/datasource/docker/).

---

### 3.80 Manifestes Kubernetes — analyser et corriger, sans jamais toucher un cluster — **à explorer**

Kubernetes entre dans le périmètre de DevDesk du côté **fichier**, pas du côté
exécution : lire des manifestes, YAML ou Helm, dans un dépôt ou un
workspace, et faire pour eux ce que §3.2 et §3.78 font déjà pour les
Dockerfiles — détecter, et corriger ce qui se corrige de façon sûre. Pas de
connexion à un cluster, pas de `kubectl`, pas de pod qui tourne : DevDesk
reste un outil qui lit et écrit des fichiers.

Lu pour cette entrée : *Docker and Kubernetes Security* (2025), chapitre 6
(« Securing Containers in Kubernetes ») et §3.6.4 (Kubescape), un Docker
Captain comme auteur.

**Premier fait vérifié, pas supposé : DevDesk détecte déjà des
misconfigurations Kubernetes, aujourd'hui, sans rien changer.**

```
$ trivy fs --scanners misconfig ./repo-avec-un-deployment.yaml
Type: kubernetes, ID: KSV-0001  "Can elevate its own privileges"
Type: kubernetes, ID: KSV-0012  "Runs as root user"
Type: kubernetes, ID: KSV-0013  Image tag ":latest" used
…
```

`trivyMisconfigArgs` (`internal/scan/trivy_args.go:169`) lance déjà `trivy fs
--scanners misconfig` sur tout workspace scanné — la même commande qui trouve
les problèmes de Dockerfile trouve, sans le savoir, les manifestes Kubernetes
qu'un dépôt contient. Vérifié en local (Trivy 0.71.2) sur un `Deployment` avec
`privileged: true` : six `KSV-*` remontent, avec span, sévérité et
`Resolution`, exactement le même format que les `DS*`/`AVD-DS-*` déjà utilisés
par le catalogue §3.78.

**Ce qui manque n'est donc pas la détection — c'est de savoir de quel dialecte
IaC vient un finding.** `TrivyResult.Type` (`internal/scan/trivy.go:20`, valeur
`"kubernetes"`, `"dockerfile"`, `"terraform"`, `"cloudformation"`, `"helm"`…)
est décodé et **jeté** : `scan.Finding` n'a aucun champ qui le porte. C'est
exactement la forme du trou que la phase A de §3.78 a refermé pour
`EndLine`/`Message`/`Status` — un champ que Trivy rend déjà et que la
construction du `Finding` ne garde pas. Sans lui, impossible de grouper les
findings par manifeste, de leur donner un libellé distinct dans l'onglet
Misconfigurations, ou d'indexer un catalogue de correctifs par dialecte.

Le texte de la décision B2 de §3.78 l'anticipait déjà sans le construire :
*« … sinon la colonne proposerait d'écrire un Dockerfile sur un onglet qui
liste aussi des manifestes Kubernetes »* (§3.78, table des décisions, ligne
1) — l'onglet existant a été conçu en sachant que ce jour viendrait.

**Le piège que §3.78 a déjà noté, et qu'il faut prendre au sérieux ici** :
*« YAML, Kubernetes et Terraform sont la classe la plus nombreuse et celle où
`Rewrite` par span ne suffit plus : la correction y est souvent ajouter une
clé dans un mapping, ce qui demande un parseur préservant indentation et
commentaires. »* Concrètement :

| Correctif | `patch.Rewrite` par span suffit ? |
|---|---|
| `image: nginx:latest` → `image: nginx:1.27` | **Oui** — remplacement de valeur, la clé existe déjà |
| `privileged: true` → `privileged: false` | **Oui** — même chose |
| Ajouter `securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` **absent** | **Non** — insérer une clé dans un mapping YAML en préservant l'indentation, les commentaires et les ancres n'est pas un remplacement de span, c'est une édition d'arbre |
| Ajouter un `NetworkPolicy` deny-all manquant | **Non** — un document YAML entier à créer |

Le projet dépend déjà de `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` (voir `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, section
Dépendances), dont le type `yaml.Node` édite un arbre en préservant les
commentaires — le candidat naturel pour la moitié des correctifs que le span
ne couvre pas, si l'étage 1 va jusque-là.

**Paysage des outils, sur le même format que §3.78** (vérifié le
2026-09-21) :

| Outil | Détecte | Corrige | Ce que ça vaut ici |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Trivy** (déjà intégré) | oui — manifestes et Helm, règles `KSV-*` | non | Rien à ajouter côté outillage : la détection existe, seul le typage du finding manque |
| **kube-linter** | oui — règles idiomatiques distinctes de Trivy (sondes de vie/prêt manquantes, requêtes de ressources absentes…) | non | Un deuxième catalogue de détection, avec un recouvrement partiel et non documenté avec Trivy — le même piège que Semgrep vs AVD noté en §3.78 |
| **Kyverno** (`kyverno apply`, règles `mutate`) | oui, hors cluster | oui — mais **réécrit la ressource entière**, pas un patch : commentaires et mise en forme perdus, ce que `patch.Rewrite` garantit justement de ne pas faire | Même réserve qu'en §3.78 |
| **Kubescape** (CNCF) | oui — manifestes (`kubescape scan --submit=false`) et cluster live, référentiels NSA-CISA/CIS/MITRE ATT&CK | non, en usage manifeste seul | Un troisième catalogue de détection ; la référence aux benchmarks (CIS, NSA-CISA) est un angle que Trivy et kube-linter n'ont pas, utile pour un rapport de conformité plutôt qu'un correctif |

Aucun outil neuf n'apporte de correction automatique sûre pour le cas général
— **exactement la même conclusion qu'en §3.78** pour les misconfigurations
Docker : le déterministe couvre un sous-ensemble fini (remplacement de
valeur), le reste est soit un patch YAML-aware à construire, soit le travail
d'un agent appelant via le MCP.

**Ce que ça donne comme découpage, par analogie directe avec §3.78 :**

- **Étage 2 (MCP), presque gratuit.** `scan_result` projette déjà les
  findings Trivy ; ajouter le type de dialecte IaC (le trou ci-dessus) et
  l'agent appelant peut déjà lire, corriger et faire re-mesurer un manifeste
  Kubernetes exactement comme il le fait pour un Dockerfile.
- **Étage 1 (catalogue maison), à dimensionner.** Un sous-ensemble
  « remplacement de valeur » (image `:latest`, `privileged: true`,
  capacités par défaut) tient dans `patch.Rewrite` sans rien construire de
  neuf. Un sous-ensemble « insertion de clé » (contextes de sécurité absents,
  network policies manquantes) demande un éditeur YAML par arbre — une pièce
  qui n'existe pas encore dans `internal/patch`.

**Hors périmètre, explicitement** : se connecter à un cluster (`kubectl`,
Kubescape en mode live, RBAC en vigueur, `etcd`), auditer un cluster qui
tourne, ou toute vérification qui suppose un `kubeconfig`. Ce que le livre
appelle « Kubernetes cluster security » (chapitre 7 : API server, kubelet,
RBAC, `etcd`) reste hors de ce que DevDesk fait — un outil qui lit des
fichiers, pas un client de cluster.

**Secrets** — noté en passant, à vérifier plutôt qu'à supposer : un `Secret`
Kubernetes en YAML n'est que de l'encodage base64, pas du chiffrement, et un
tel fichier commité est un secret en clair pour Gitleaks. Comme tout fichier
texte d'un workspace scanné, il devrait déjà être couvert par le scan de
secrets existant — à confirmer par un test plutôt qu'à écrire ici comme un
fait.

**Ouvert, pas tranché :**

| # | Question |
|---|---|
| 1 | Où DevDesk cherche des manifestes Kubernetes dans un workspace — tout `*.yaml`/`*.yml` (risque de faux positifs sur un YAML qui n'est pas un manifeste), ou une heuristique sur le contenu (`apiVersion`/`kind`, ce que Trivy fait déjà en interne) |
| 2 | Les charts Helm sont dans le périmètre du livre (Trivy les scanne aussi) — DevDesk les lit-il tels quels, ou seulement leur rendu (`helm template`), ce qui réintroduirait une dépendance externe |
| 3 | L'onglet : une nouvelle colonne « dialecte » sur l'onglet Misconfigurations existant (ce que la décision B2 de §3.78 anticipait), ou un onglet séparé si le volume de findings Kubernetes s'avère dominer |
| 4 | kube-linter et Kubescape apportent-ils des règles que Trivy n'a pas, au point de justifier un troisième outil — à mesurer sur des manifestes réels avant de trancher, pas à deviner depuis la doc |

3169	## 4.4.1 Use Slim Images
3170	
3171	The base image should be as small as possible. Many base images have slim versions. For example the Node version (based on Debian Bookworm) is 1.1 GB in size, while the slim version is 269 MB. The Debian Docker image itself is 50 MB, while the slim version is 30 MB. The Alpine Linux image is 5 MB in size, as it is a super tiny Linux distribution. This is why many Docker images are based on Alpine Linux. Alpine Linux is a security-oriented, lightweight Linux distribution based on musl libc and busybox, instead of GNU libc (glibc) and coreutils that are used in most Linux distributions like Debian and Ubuntu.
3172	
3173	The package manager of Alpine Linux is called apk. It's similar to apt and yum that are used in Debian and Red Hat-based distributions respectively, but you have to check the package names as they might differ between package managers. We'll get to that later.
3174	
3175	In 2025, many production teams now prefer distroless or Wolfi-based images for even smaller attack surfaces. These contain only the runtime libraries and no shell or package manager.
3176	
3177	## 4.4.2 Build Minimal Images (Distroless or Scratch)
3178	
3179	Distroless images are minimal runtime bases (no shell or package manager) that still include required runtime libraries (e.g., glibc). By contrast, scratch is literally empty. Use scratch only for fully static binaries; use distroless when you need a minimal userspace without the shell and tools.
3180	
3181	## 1 FROM scratch
3182	
3183	This is especially useful when you have a compiled language, and your final result is a binary file. One might ask, why use containers if our final result is a single binary file that can be executed natively? Well, because still the binary running in the container is isolated and can be orchestrated alongside your other services using Kubernetes.
3184	
3185	Well, of course another benefit is that you can use Docker tooling with it, for example, for generating an SBOM from the build stage, as we mentioned in Chapter 2.

3187	## 4.4.3 Use the Right Tag
3188	
3189	When choosing a base image, it's important to choose the right tag. The tag should be as specific as possible. For example, instead of using ubuntu:latest, use ubuntu:24.04 . This way, you can be sure that the base image is always 24.04. That being said, it's possible to publish a new image with the same tag. Returning to our previous example, the ubuntu :24.04 image can be updated with a new version of Ubuntu 24.04, with security patches and bug fixes. So, if you use ubuntu:24.04 in your Dockerfile, you can be sure that the base image is always 24.04, but you can't be sure that it's always the same version of 24.04.
3190	
3191	That being said, you can trust the Ubuntu image versions, because that's an official image and it's being checked by many parties. However, if you're using a custom image, you should be careful about the tag you use. It's always possible that the maintainer of the image updates the tag with a new version of the image, which might break your application.
3192	
3193	If you want to be sure that the base image is always the same, you can use the SHA256 digest of the image. The SHA256 digest is a unique identifier for the image and is calculated based on the content of the image. If the content of the image changes, the SHA256 digest will change too.
3194	
3195	Let’s see how to get the SHA256 digest of an image for the Ubuntu 24.04 image:
3196	
3197	```
3198	$ docker pull ubuntu:24.04 $ docker inspect --format='{{index ␣ .RepoDigests␣0}}' ubuntu:24.04
3199	```
3200	
3201	The output of the docker inspect command is the SHA256 digest of the image. You can use this digest in your Dockerfile:
3202	
3203	```
3204	1 FROM ubuntu@sha256:7 a47b3f6b8a0e044a5f0b9c3f60d64b59b0a1d5a3f4c7705c5c0a1b3d8f3eaa9
3205	```
3206	
3207	That's something you should decide for yourself. Do you want to use exactly the same image every time, or do you want to get the security updates.
3208	
3209	A middle ground is to make a copy of the images you use in your private registry. This way, you have control over the images you use, and you can update them when you want. There are many vendors that offer private registries, Docker Hub itself, GitHub's Container Registry, JFrog, et cetera. One can also host their own private registry using Docker Registry or Harbor.
3210	
3211	Another issue one might face when using base images, is that the supply chain of the base image might get compromised. This means that our lovely Jack "the Bitcoin Miner" has managed to tamper with the base image and add a bitcoin miner to it. This is a serious issue, as it can lead to a compromised application and a compromised production environment.
3212	
3213	The modern solution for this problem is to verify signatures using Notation (Notary v2) or Cosign. These tools ensure that images you pull are exactly those published by the trusted source.
3214	
3215	In Chapter 9, we will talk about standards and best practices when building secure Docker images.

3217	## 4.5 Sign Docker Images
3218	
3219	In 2025, Docker Content Trust and Notary v1 have been replaced by Notation (Notary v2) and Sigstore Cosign. These tools support modern OCI artifacts (images, SBOMs, and provenance attestations) and are widely integrated into CI/CD pipelines.
3220	
3221	Signing an image with Notation looks like this:
3222	
3223	```
3224	$ notation sign --key mykey myregistry/myimage:1.0.0 $ notation verify myregistry/myimage:1.0.0 Using Cosign is also straightforward: $ cosign sign myregistry/myimage:1.0.0 $ cosign verify myregistry/myimage:1.0.0
3225	```
3226	
3227	Both tools attach signatures to the registry. CI/CD policy gates, registry policy engines, and Kubernetes admission controllers can require valid signatures so that only trusted images are deployed.
3228	
3229	Key tip . Always sign your images and the SBOMs/provenance attestations created during the build. This ensures end-to-end supply chain integrity.
3230	
3231	Modern pipelines increasingly use keyless signing (e.g., Cosign with OIDC in CI) so builds can sign artifacts with short-lived identities tied to the workflow run—eliminating the need to manage long-lived private keys.

3233	## 4.6 Installing OS Dependencies
3234	
3235	Earlier in the chapter, we talked about the base image and how it should be as small as possible. We also talked about Alpine Linux and how it's a good choice for a base image. Alpine Linux uses apk as its package manager, which is similar to Debian's apt and Red Hat's yum .
3236	
3237	In a Dockerfile, after the base image is specified, the next step is to install the dependencies. The dependencies are installed using the package manager of the base image. Let's say you want to install curl in your Dockerfile. If you're using Alpine Linux, you can install it using apk:
3238	
3239	```
3240	1 FROM alpine:latest 2 3 RUN apk add --no-cache curl
3241	```
3242	
3243	If you’re using Ubuntu or Debian, you can install it using apt:
3244	
3245	```
3246	1 FROM ubuntu:24.04 2 3 RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && apt-get clean && rm -rf / var/lib/apt/lists/* /var/cache/apt/archives/*
3247	```
3248	
3249	There are a few points to consider:
3250	
3251	- You first need to run apt-get update to update the package list. With Alpine, if you use apk add --no-cache ..., you don't need a prior apk update because the index is fetched and not persisted.
3252	- You need to use apt-get install instead of apt install. The apt command is recommended to be used when you're using the interactive shell. The apt-get command is recommended to be used when you're writing a script.
3253	- You need to use the -y flag to automatically answer yes to the prompt, otherwise the installation will fail.
3254	- On Debian/Ubuntu, after installing packages, run apt-get clean and remove cached indexes and .deb files (e.g., rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* /var/cache/ apt/archives/*) to keep the image small.
3255	- On Alpine, use apk add --no-cache ... to avoid persisting the index. Debian/Ubuntu do not have an --no-cache flag in apt-get .
3256	
3257	If you want to install multiple packages or specific versions:
3258	
3259	```
3260	1 # Base image pinned to a specific release (pin to a digest if you need immutability) 2 FROM ubuntu:24.04 3 4 # Optionally: point /etc/apt/sources.list to a snapshot/mirror you control for full reproducibility. 5 RUN apt-get update && \ 6 apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ 7 curl=<curl_version_from_your_repo> \ 8 wget=<wget_version_from_your_repo> && \ 9 apt-mark hold curl wget && \ 10 apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* /var/cache/apt/archives/*
3261	```
3262	
3263	## Notice that:
3264	
3265	- --no-install-recommends keeps the image slim by avoiding optional packages.
3266	
3267	- All commands are in one RUN to avoid stale caches.
3268	- There is no --no-cache option with apt-get .
3269	
3270	Some applications have language-specific OS packages. For example, sometimes it's easier to install Python packages with apt instead of pip. In such cases, separate the package list into multiple lines for readability and git-blame-friendliness.
3271	
3272	Unlike OS dependencies, it is a big deal for application dependencies to have a specific version when installed.

3274	## 4.7 Installing Application Dependencies
3275	
3276	Application dependencies are usually listed in manifest/lock files. Examples include:
3277	
3278	- requirements.txt for Python
3279	- Gemfile for Ruby
3280	- package.json for Node.js
3281	- go.mod for Go
3282	- pom.xml for Java
3283	- etc.
3284	
3285	There are usually two types of application dependencies; the ones that must be present in the container and the ones that are only needed for building the application. Let's start with an interpreted language like Python.
3286	
3287	## 4.7.1 Interpreted Languages
3288	
3289	Interpreted languages are languages that are executed by an interpreter. This means that the code is not compiled into a binary file, and the source code is executed directly by the interpreter. Because it all happens at runtime, there are a lot of dependencies that need to be present in the container to run the application.
3290	
3291	Examples of such languages are Python, Ruby, and Node.js. Well, I didn't want to list PHP here because I don't like it, but it's also an interpreted language.
3292	
3293	In Python, as we discussed in the previous chapter, the dependencies are usually listed in a file like requirements.txt. The requirements.txt file contains the name of the packages and their versions. To install these dependencies, the file needs to be available to Docker. This can be done using the COPY instruction:
3294	
3295	```
3296	1 FROM python:3.11.3-slim 2 3 WORKDIR /app 4 5 COPY requirements.txt . 6 7 RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt 8 9 COPY . . 10 11 CMD ["python", "main.py"]
3297	```
3298	
3299	The first COPY instruction copies the requirements.txt file from the build context to the image. Then the packages are installed using the pip install command. The COPY instruction is used again to copy the rest of the files to the image.
3300	
3301	The dependency list is copied in a separate COPY layer, and the install runs in its own RUN layer. This is because Docker caches the layers, and if you install the packages in a separate RUN instruction, Docker will use the cached layer and the packages won't be installed again if there are no changes to the requirements.txt file. To further enhance the package installation, you can use mounting:
3302	
3303	```
3304	1 RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \ 2 --mount=type=bind,source=requirements.txt,target=requirements.txt \ 3 python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
3305	```
3306	
3307	Using the --mount option of the RUN instruction, the requirements.txt file is mounted and the packages are installed. By mounting the requirements.txt file, it is not copied into the image, but is made available to the Docker daemon.
3308	
3309	Here, an extra cache is also mounted to cache the packages. This will speed up the next builds, as the packages are cached and don't need to be downloaded again.
3310	
3311	Multi-stage builds are also useful for interpreted languages. For example, a Node.js or Python app can install build-only tooling (linters, compilers, asset bundlers, native build deps) in a "builder" stage and then copy only the runtime artifacts into a minimal final image. This keeps the production image smaller and reduces the attack surface by excluding dev tooling.
3312	
3313	## 4.7.2 Compiled Languages
3314	
3315	The main difference here is that the dependencies are compiled and the compiled binaries are copied to the image. Let's take C++ as an example:
3316	
3317	```
3318	1 FROM ubuntu:24.04 AS build 2 3 RUN apt-get update && \ 4 apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential && \ 5 rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* 6 7 WORKDIR /app 8 COPY hello.cpp . 9 10 # Ensure a fully static binary suitable for `FROM scratch` 11 RUN g++ -O2 -static -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -o hello hello.cpp && \ 12 file hello # should report: "statically linked" 13 14 # --------------------15 FROM scratch 16 COPY --from=build /app/hello /hello 17 CMD ["/hello"]
3319	```
3320	
3321	This is a multi-stage Dockerfile. The first stage is used to build the application and the second stage is used to run the application. The final image is the result of the final stage, hence in this example, it will contain only the hello binary, no shell, no package manager, nothing.
3322	
3323	In this example, the hello.cpp file is copied to the image and then compiled using g++ . The -static flag is used to statically link the libraries, so that the final binary doesn't depend on any shared libraries.
3324	
3325	Here, we didn't need to install any third-party libraries, as the example is a simple "Hello, World!" program. Either way, the dependencies are installed in the first stage and won't end up in the final image. That's the main difference between interpreted and compiled languages in Dockerfiles.
3326	
3327	The dependencies that are used to build the application are as important as the dependencies that are used to run the application. As the build dependencies are not present in
3328	
3329	the final image, they won't be scanned for vulnerabilities by default, mostly because the vulnerability scanners can't know about them. 5
