3331	## 4.8 Generating SBOM Upon Build
3332	
3333	We introduced SBOMs in the previous chapter. We talked about how they can be used to detect vulnerabilities in the third-party libraries. An SBOM generated for a Docker image will contain all the third-party libraries in the base image, in the OS packages, and in the application dependencies.
3334	
3335	When building a Docker image, you can generate an SBOM and attach it to the image:
3336	
3337	```
3338	$ docker buildx build -t c-hello --sbom=true .
3339	```
3340	
3341	--provenance=true The short version is the following: $ docker build -t c-hello --sbom=true .
3342	
3343	The SBOM is generated and attached to the image. To verify the SBOM generation, you can do the build again and set the output to be of file format:
3344	
3345	```
3346	$ docker buildx build \ -t c-hello:sbom \ --sbom=true \ --provenance=true \ --output type=local,dest=out .
3347	```
3348	
3349	If you look into the out directory, you should see a file called sbom.spdx.json. The SPDX format is a standard format for SBOMs and stands for Software Package Data Exchange.
3350	
3351	To take the earlier stages of the build into account, you can use Docker arguments:
3352	
3353	```
3354	1 ARG BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_CONTEXT=true 2 FROM ubuntu:24.04 AS build 3 ...
3355	```
3356	
3357	5 Here, Go is an exception, as the third-party libraries are compiled into the binary and can be detected by the scanners. This is not the case for C and C++ languages, as the third-party libraries are linked dynamically and can't be detected by the scanners.
3358	
3359	Now, the out directory contains sbom.spdx.json plus an additional context SBOM/attestation file (the exact name can vary by BuildKit version).
3360	
3361	The SBOM generator behind Docker, at the time of writing this book, is Syft. Syft is able to detect third-party Go libraries from the Go binaries, but that's not possible for other languages like C and C++.
3362	
3363	Modern Docker BuildKit supports first-class SBOMs and provenance attestations. Enable them during builds with --sbom=true and --provenance=true. These can be signed with Cosign or Notation and stored in the registry next to the image. Docker Scout continuously analyzes SBOMs for new CVEs, ensuring that even after your image is deployed, you are notified about newly discovered vulnerabilities.
3364	
3365	An alternative is Cosign, which is a CNCF tool that allows you to sign Docker images as well as their SBOM attestations. The SBOM attestation generated by Cosign is stored in the registry differently than the BuildKit attestation. Some tools might pick up one or the other. For example, Docker Scout can read both, and SigStore's admission controller can read the Cosign SBOM attestation.
3366	
3367	One large advantage of using BuildKit SBOMs is that they are generated during the build process, so they can be used to detect vulnerabilities in the third-party libraries before the image is pushed to the registry. If you want to sign this SBOM with Cosign, you can manually get the BuildKit SBOM attestation (e.g. using the output directory), sign it with Cosign, and then push it to the registry.
3368	
3369	We will get back to the SBOM attestations, but let's first talk about one of the most overlooked security issues in Docker images: running as non-root.
3370	
3371	## 4.9 Running as Non-root
3372	
3373	In the first chapter we talked about Linux kernel namespaces and mentioned that one namespace that is often not enabled by default in container runtimes is the user namespace. The user namespace is used to map the root user in the container to a non-root user on the host. By default, Docker runs containers as UID 0 inside the container; unless user namespaces are enabled, this is also UID 0 on the host UID map. Kernel isolation still prevents direct host control, but if a container-escape vulnerability is exploited, that UID mapping can translate into host-level root impact. This is why it's recommended to run the container as a non-root user.
3374	
3375	To run the container as non-root, you need to specify the user using the USER instruction:
3376	
3377	```
3378	1 FROM ubuntu:24.04 2 3 RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y iputils-ping 4 5 RUN groupadd --system appgroup && \ 6 useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid appgroup \ 7 --home-dir /nonexistent --shell /usr/sbin/nologin --no-create-home appuser 8 USER appuser 9 10 CMD ["ping", "google.com"]
3379	```
3380	
3381	The useradd/groupadd commands create a dedicated system user and group for the app. The --system and --no-create-home flags avoid creating a real login account, and the --shell /usr/sbin/nologin setting disallows interactive shells. The USER instruction then switches the runtime user for the container.
3382	
3383	Let’s build the image and run it:
3384	
3385	```
3386	$ docker build -t non-root-ping . $ docker run --rm non-root-ping
3387	```
3388	
3389	Would you expect it to work or not? Well, drum roll please, it works! It's similar to the ping command on the host that can be used by non-root users. The ping binary has the necessary privilege to open raw sockets (on modern distros this is typically via Linux capabilities such as CAP\_NET\_RAW, historically via setuid), so it can run successfully even when the container itself runs as a non-root user—provided the container's default capability set includes CAP\_NET\_RAW (Docker's default does, unless you drop it).
3390	
3391	Let's try another example. Let's create a hello world container that prints "Hello, world!" to the standard output every 5 seconds:
3392	
3393	```
3394	1 FROM alpine:latest 2 3 RUN addgroup -S appgroup && \ 4 adduser -S -D -H -h /nonexistent -s /sbin/nologin -G appgroup appuser 5 USER appuser 6
3395	```
3396	
3397	```
3398	7 CMD while true; do echo "Hello, world!"; sleep 5; done Let's build the image and run it: $ docker build -t non-root-hello . $ docker run --name non-root-hello --rm non-root-hello Use another terminal to get into the container: $ docker exec -it non-root-hello sh Now let's try installing a package: $ apk add curl
3399	```
3400	
3401	You should get an error saying ERROR: Unable to lock database: Permission denied . This is because the apk command is not a setuid program. So, effectively, the user in the container doesn't have root privileges and can't install packages.
3402	
3403	The best practice for creating a non-root user upon build is the following:
3404	
3405	```
3406	1 ARG UID=10001 2 RUN adduser \ 3 --disabled-password \ 4 --gecos "" \ 5 --home "/nonexistent" \ 6 --shell "/usr/sbin/nologin" \ 7 --no-create-home \ 8 --uid "${UID}" \ 9 appuser
3407	```
3408	
3409	Well, that’s a lot of flags. Let’s go through them one by one:
3410	
3411	- --disabled-password: This flag is used to disable the password for the user. This is because the user is not supposed to login to the container.
3412	- --gecos "": This flag is used to set the user's information. The user's information is usually used for the user's full name, office number, and phone number, which are not needed here.
3413	- --home "/nonexistent": This flag is used to set the user's home directory. Setting a real home directory allows the user to write files to the home directory, which is not needed here.
3414	
3415	- --shell "/usr/sbin/nologin" (on Alpine use "/sbin/nologin"): This flag is used to set the user's shell. Setting a real shell allows the user to run commands, which is not needed here. Giving the user a shell is also a security risk, as the user can run commands in the container.
3416	- --no-create-home: This flag is used to not create the user's home directory. This is because the user is not supposed to write files to the home directory.
3417	- --uid "${UID}": This flag is used to set the user's UID. The UID is set to a non-root UID. The UID is set using an argument, so it can be overridden during the build.
3418	
3419	The default UID is set to 10001. Setting the UID to a non-root UID is important, because if the UID is set to 0, the user will have root privileges. The UID 10001 usually doesn't exist on the host, so it's a good choice for the UID. On the host machine, one can check the UID of the user using the id command:
3420	
3421	$ id
3422	
3423	Also, /etc/passwd contains the list of users on the host.
3424	
3425	$ cat /etc/passwd
3426	
3427	Note . The exact nobody entry varies by OS (e.g., UID 65534 on many Linux distros and -2 on macOS). The key idea is that a non-login user lacks a real shell and home directory, similar to the user we create in the Dockerfile.
3428	
3429	Each line contains the following fields:
3430	
3431	- Username
3432	- Password
3433	- UID (User ID)
3434	- GID (Group ID)
3435	- User information
3436	- Home directory
3437	- Shell

3439	## 4.10 Docker Init
3440	
3441	Writing a standard Dockerfile can be boilerplate. You need to specify the base image, install the dependencies, and specify the command to run. And if you want to take security into account, your Dockerfile will be even longer. That's why Docker has introduced Docker Init . 6
3442	
3443	A few days back I wrote on Twitter that Docker Init is great because it's not based on LLMs, so it's deterministic. Docker liked it and made a post about it, hashtagging #DockerCaptainInsights 7 .

3446

3449	```
3450	
3451	I ran it for a Python project and it created the following Dockerfile:
3452	
3453	```
3454	1 ## syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 2 3 ## Comments are provided throughout this file to help you get started. 4 ## If you need more help, visit the Dockerfile reference guide at 5 ## https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/ 6 7 ARG PYTHON_VERSION=3.11.3 8 FROM python:${PYTHON_VERSION}-slim as base 9 10 ## Prevents Python from writing pyc files. 11 ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 12 13 ## Keeps Python from buffering stdout and stderr to avoid situations where 14 ## the application crashes without emitting any logs due to buffering. 15 ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 16 17 WORKDIR /app 18
3455	```
3456	
3457	6 Here "Docker Init" refers to the CLI tool that scaffolds Dockerfiles; it is not the container "init process" or the --init flag used at runtime to reap zombies.
3458	
3459	7 https://x.com/Docker/status/1934618217990754462
3460	
3461	```
3462	19 ## Create a non-privileged user that the app will run under. 20 ## See https://docs.docker.com/develop/develop-images/dockerfile_best-practices/#user 21 ARG UID=10001 22 RUN adduser \ 23 --disabled-password \ 24 --gecos "" \ 25 --home "/nonexistent" \ 26 --shell "/usr/sbin/nologin" \ 27 --no-create-home \ 28 --uid "${UID}" \ 29 appuser 30 31 ## Download dependencies as a separate step to take advantage of Docker's caching. 32 ## Leverage a cache mount to /root/.cache/pip to speed up subsequent builds. 33 ## Leverage a bind mount to requirements.txt to avoid having to copy them into 34 ## into this layer. 35 RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \ 36 --mount=type=bind,source=requirements.txt,target=requirements.txt \ 37 python -m pip install -r requirements.txt 38 39 ## Switch to the non-privileged user to run the application. 40 USER appuser 41 42 ## Copy the source code into the container. 43 COPY backend . 44 45 ## Copy PostgreSQL root certificates into the container. 46 COPY root.crt $HOME/.postgresql/root.crt 47 COPY root.crt /nonexistent/.postgresql/root.crt 48 49 ## Expose the port that the application listens on. 50 EXPOSE 8000 51 52 ## Run the application.
3463	```

3466	53 CMD ["gunicorn", "backend.wsgi", "--bind=0.0.0.0:8000"]
3467	```

3470	
3471	- ARG PYTHON\_VERSION=3.11.3: This is an argument that can be overridden during the build. The default value is 3.11.3. This is good practice, as you won't need to change the Dockerfile if you want to change the Python version.

It's named after Gordon Freeman, because we love killing zombie processes! 8
3484	
3485	Knowing best practices is still important, as the generated Dockerfile might not be secure, or might not be optimized for you.
3486	
3487	## 4.11 Building Docker Images in CI/CD
3488	
3489	Docker images are usually the final artifact of a project. The Docker image is built and pushed to a registry, and then it's deployed to a Kubernetes cluster. The workflow is usually like this:
3490	
3491	1. The developer pushes the code to their feature branch on the git repository.
3492	
3493	8 It's actually named after Gordon the Tortoise, Docker's mascot, but I like the Half-Life story better.
3494	
3495	2. The CI pipeline is triggered to run some checks.
3496	3. After some reviews, the branch is merged to the main branch.
3497	4. The CI pipeline is triggered to build the Docker image and push it to the registry.
3498	5. The CD pipeline deploys the Docker image to the Kubernetes cluster.
3499	
3500	The CI pipeline does much more than run tests. It is also responsible for supply chain security. In 2025, a secure pipeline should:
3501	
3502	- Build Docker images using BuildKit with --sbom and --provenance .
3503	- Sign the resulting image and attestations with Cosign or Notation.
3504	- Scan the image using Docker Scout or Trivy and post results into the pull/merge request.
3505	- Fail or block merges if new high/critical vulnerabilities are introduced.
3506	
3507	Usually, there are many vulnerabilities in the third-party libraries. It's a good practice to catch the ones with higher severity and report them in the pull/merge request, otherwise, the important vulnerabilities might be missed in the noise.
3508	
3509	## 4.11.1 Enforcing No-Vulnerabilities Policy
3510	
3511	One could set a policy to not allow any vulnerabilities of a certain severity in the Docker image. The CI job that checks the CVEs in the dependencies can fail if there are any vulnerabilities of that severity. This will force the developer to fix the vulnerabilities before merging the pull/merge request. It's not a good practice to enforce this rule for all the vulnerabilities, as there are usually many vulnerabilities in the third-party libraries and it's not possible to fix all of them.
3512	
3513	You might want to start adapting no-vulnerabilities policy for an existing project with many vulnerabilities. In this case, you can start with a policy that checks whether you introduced any new vulnerabilities of a certain severity. This way, the next person who wants to create a pull/merge request, won't need to fix the vulnerabilities that are already there, but will need to fix the ones that they introduced.
3514	
3515	You might also want to whitelist some vulnerabilities. For example, if you're using a library that has a vulnerability, but you're not using the vulnerable part of the library, you might want to whitelist that vulnerability.
3516	
3517	## 4.12 Automating Vulnerability Fixes
3518	
3519	Fixing vulnerabilities might be as easy as updating the version of the library. But, it might also be as hard as rewriting the code that uses the vulnerable part of the library, or changing a library altogether, because it's not maintained anymore. The easy parts can be automated. For example, NPM, the package manager for Node.js, has a command called npm audit fix that can be used to fix the vulnerabilities in the dependencies. You could create a scheduled job that runs this command and creates a pull/merge request if there are any changes.
3520	
3521	There are many tools that can be used to automate the vulnerability fixes. Snyk for example would create a pull/merge request if there are any vulnerabilities in the dependencies of the project. There is also a tool called Dependabot that can be used to automate the dependency updates. Dependabot is now owned by GitHub and is available as a GitHub Action. But as of now, a live person still needs to review the pull/merge request and merge it. The tools are not smart enough, and they rely on things like semantic versioning to update the dependencies.
3522	
3523	We talked about semantic versioning in the previous chapter, but let's recap it here. Semantic Versioning (or SemVer) is a versioning scheme that specifies how the version number of a library should be incremented. The version number is usually in the format of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH .
3524	
3525	The rules say that if the library has breaking changes, the major version should be incremented. This way, if the new update of the library has breaking changes, the users of the library will know that they need to change their code to use the new version. But, the rules are not always followed. Sometimes, the minor version is incremented, but there are breaking changes. And the tool will update the dependency, breaking the code.
3526	
3527	## 4.12.1 Scheduled Vulnerability Scans
3528	
3529	The vulnerability scanners can be used to scan the Docker images periodically. This way, you can be notified if there are any new vulnerabilities in the Docker image. With the SBOMs available for the Docker images, you know exactly which third-party libraries are used in the Docker image and when a new CVE is published for one of them, you can be notified. Docker Scout is trying to achieve exactly that.
3530	
3531	## 4.12.2 Docker Image Security Offered by Registries
3532	
3533	Many Docker image registries offer security features. Docker Hub and JFrog are two examples. It's important to bear in mind that these features usually use the SBOMs attached to the images to detect vulnerabilities. So if the SBOMs are generated during the build, more vulnerabilities can be detected.
3534	
3535	## 4.13 Conclusion
3536	
3537	In this chapter, we explored what it really takes to build Docker images that are secure by design. We discussed how to pick trusted, minimal base images, how to install dependencies safely, and why running as a non‑root user is no longer optional. We also covered how modern tooling like BuildKit, SBOMs, Notation, and Cosign have changed the way we think about container supply chain security.
3538	
3539	The key message is simple: an image that isn't maintained becomes a liability. New CVEs are discovered every week, and the fastest way to close these gaps is to rebuild images regularly with up‑to‑date bases and dependencies. This is why SBOMs and automated scans are so important: they tell you exactly what you're shipping so you can react quickly when a vulnerability appears.
3540	
3541	And don't forget the human factor. It's tempting to "just make it work" once and leave the same image running for months or even years, but that's a trap. If you care about the safety of your production clusters, make a habit of rebuilding and resigning your images. Security is not a one‑off event; it's a living process.
3542	
3543	In the next chapter, we'll take this one step further and see how to weave these best practices into your CI/CD pipelines, so that security becomes automatic, repeatable, and enforceable - not an afterthought.
3544	
3545	## 4.14 Exercises
3546	
3547	1. Use Docker Init on a compiled project to generate a Dockerfile. Is it a multi-stage file? Read through the Dockerfile and compare with the example given in this chapter.
3548	2. Is the generated Dockerfile using a non-root user?
3549	3. Use BuildKit to generate SBOM for all the stages. Store it locally.
3550	
3551	4. Build the image again. Use Cosign to sign the image and the generated SBOM. How was the signing procedure different from that of Notary?
3552	5. Use Docker Scout to check the image for CVEs. Does it include packages from the build stage?
3553

content.text:
Oui, en creusant le chapitre 4 (« Secure Docker Image Building Practices ») et en vérifiant chaque point contre ce que Trivy détecte déjà dans le pipeline de DevDesk, j'ai trouvé une lacune concrète et vérifiée, plus deux pistes plus larges non vérifiées en détail.

**Vérifiée — un vrai trou, rien ne le couvre aujourd'hui :**
- **Fuite de secrets par le contexte de build.** Le livre insiste : un `COPY . .` sans `.dockerignore` envoie tout le répertoire au démon, y compris un `.env`, `credentials.json`, `.git`. Testé en local : ni le scanner de misconfiguration Trivy (`--scanners misconfig`) ni le scanner de secrets (`--scanners secret`) ne signalent l'absence de `.dockerignore` ou un `COPY` large sans exclusion — c'est un contrôle statique que rien dans le pipeline actuel ne fait. Le scan de secrets existant (`trivy image --scanners secret`) ne rattraperait le problème qu'après build, sur l'image finale — pas avant.

**Déjà couvert — vérifié pour éviter de proposer un doublon :**
- Utilisateur root, absence de `HEALTHCHECK`, `apt-get` sans `--no-install-recommends` : Trivy les détecte déjà aujourd'hui dans le scan de workspace, testé en local sur un Dockerfile minimal.
- Le motif exact de création d'utilisateur non-root que le livre recommande (`adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" --home "/nonexistent" --shell "/usr/sbin/nologin" --no-create-home --uid`) est déjà celui que le correctif racine de §3.78 (B1) écrit.

**Vues mais pas creusées — plus larges, hors du format "une règle, un correctif" :**
- Vérification de signature (Cosign/Notation) et de SBOM avant d'utiliser une image de base — pas une détection de misconfiguration, plutôt une nouvelle catégorie de contrôle (intégrité de la chaîne d'appro), à part de la remédiation actuelle.
- Préférer les images Wolfi/distroless dès le départ — moins une remédiation d'image existante (§3.2 compare des tags d'une même ligne) qu'un choix de démarrage, qui toucherait plutôt le catalogue de templates (`internal/template`) que la remédiation.

Je n'ai pas encore écrit d'entrée backlog pour ces points — tu veux que j'en ajoute une pour la fuite par contexte de build (§3.81), ou que je creuse d'abord les deux pistes plus larges avant de les formuler ?

### 3.81 Fuite de secrets par le contexte de build — aucun outil du pipeline ne la voit — **à explorer**

Trouvé en lisant le chapitre 4 (« Secure Docker Image Building Practices »),
et vérifié en local plutôt que supposé : un `COPY . .` sans `.dockerignore`
envoie tout le répertoire au démon de build, y compris un `.env`, un
`credentials.json`, un `.git` complet. Un test sur un Dockerfile minimal
(`FROM alpine:3.20` + `COPY . /app`, un `.env` à côté) montre que **ni**
`trivy fs --scanners misconfig` **ni** `trivy fs --scanners secret` ne
signalent quoi que ce soit — pas d'avertissement sur l'absence de
`.dockerignore`, pas de détection du fichier qui serait copié. C'est un
contrôle statique que rien dans le pipeline actuel ne fait.

**Pourquoi le scan de secrets existant ne suffit pas à couvrir ce cas.**
`trivyMisconfigArgs`/`trivySecretArgs` (`internal/scan/trivy_args.go:169`,
`:140`) scannent le **répertoire source**, avant tout build — ils ne voient
jamais ce qu'un `COPY` copierait réellement dans l'image. Le seul scan qui
verrait le fichier une fois dans l'image est `trivy image --scanners secret`
(`trivy_args.go:155`), qui suppose une image déjà construite — hors de portée
d'une analyse de Dockerfile statique. Et même là, une valeur générique comme
`SECRET=abc123` ne matche aucun pattern de secret connu (clé AWS, clé privée,
etc.) — testé, aucune alerte.

**Ce qui serait à vérifier avant de scoper plus loin :**

1. Une règle statique est-elle raisonnable : présence d'un `COPY . .` (ou
   équivalent large) **et** absence de `.dockerignore`, ou `.dockerignore`
   qui n'exclut pas `.git`/`.env`/patterns usuels de secrets. Un faux positif
   plausible : un projet qui n'a simplement rien à cacher dans son contexte.
2. Est-ce une détection seule (avertissement dans l'onglet Misconfigurations,
   sans AVD id puisque Trivy ne la fournit pas) ou un correctif proposé
   (générer un `.dockerignore` par défaut) — la seconde option écrit un
   **nouveau fichier**, pas une édition de span sur un fichier existant, donc
   une forme différente de ce que `patch.Rewrite` fait aujourd'hui.
3. Est-ce que cela vaut la peine par rapport au scan de secrets déjà présent
   sur le dépôt — si un `.env` est déjà commité, Gitleaks/Trivy secret le
   trouvent indépendamment du Dockerfile ; le risque propre à cette entrée
   est le fichier **non commité mais présent localement** (ignoré par git,
   pas par `docker build`).

Sources vérifiées le 2026-09-21 :
*Docker and Kubernetes Security* (§4.3, sur `.dockerignore` et le contexte de
build), test local (Trivy 0.71.2, `trivy fs --scanners misconfig,secret`).

---

### 3.82 Vérifier la signature et le SBOM d'une image de base avant de la recommander — **à explorer**

Trouvé au chapitre 4 (§4.5, §4.8) : la chaîne d'approvisionnement d'une image
de base peut être compromise sans qu'aucune CVE ne le révèle — un registre
compromis republie une image sous le même tag, avec un contenu altéré. La
défense recommandée est la vérification de signature (Cosign, Notation) et la
présence d'un SBOM signé, pas un scan de vulnérabilités, qui ne voit que ce
qui est déjà catalogué.

**Ce n'est pas une extension du catalogue de misconfigurations** — c'est une
question différente de celles que §3.2 et §3.78 posent (« cette CVE est-elle
corrigée », « cette règle passe-t-elle ») : « ce contenu est-il bien celui que
le mainteneur a publié ». §3.2 choisit déjà un candidat de base image
(`internal/remediation/tags.go`) sans jamais consulter cette question — un
candidat plus récent pourrait tout aussi bien être non signé, ou signé par
une identité inattendue.

**Pas creusé plus loin ici, volontairement** — la portée est plus grande
qu'une règle de catalogue : elle suppose un appel réseau vers le registre
(`cosign verify`, ou lire une attestation OCI), une politique de confiance
(quelles clés/identités sont acceptées), et une décision sur ce que DevDesk
fait d'une image non signée (avertir seulement, ou refuser de la proposer
comme candidat). Trois questions qui ne se répondent pas depuis la lecture
d'un livre.

Sources vérifiées le 2026-09-21 :
*Docker and Kubernetes Security* (§4.5, §4.8),
[Sigstore Cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/overview/),
[Notation (Notary v2)](https://notaryproject.dev/docs/).

---

### 3.83 Préférer les images minimales (Wolfi, distroless) dès la création d'un dépôt — **à explorer**

Trouvé au chapitre 4 (§4.4, §4.4.1, §4.4.2) : au-delà de corriger une image de
base existante (§3.2), le livre recommande de partir d'une base minimale —
Wolfi ou distroless plutôt qu'Alpine ou Debian slim — pour réduire la surface
dès le départ. Une remédiation ne peut proposer que « une version plus récente
de la même image » ; elle ne change jamais de famille de base.

**Le point d'accroche existe déjà, vérifié plutôt que supposé.** Un template
du catalogue (`internal/template`) est une référence vers un dépôt externe —
`Entry.Source` (`internal/template/template.go:36`) — pas un contenu que
DevDesk écrit ; impossible d'y imposer une base au moment de la création.
Mais `internal/ui/templates/scan.go` matérialise déjà un template dans
`~/.devdesk/cache/template-scan/<slug>` et le scanne « comme n'importe quel
autre » avant qu'un dépôt en soit créé — donc le Dockerfile d'un template
**passe déjà** par le même scan de misconfiguration qu'un dépôt normal. Le
point d'accroche est informatif, pas correctif : un avertissement sur la
famille de base au moment du scan de template, pas une réécriture.

**Pas creusé plus loin ici** :

1. Trivy n'a pas de règle « base non minimale » — cela resterait à détecter
   autrement (taille de l'image de base, ou une liste de familles connues
   pour être lourdes) ; à vérifier avant de supposer que c'est simple.
2. La distinction entre « corriger un dépôt existant » (§3.2, changer de
   version) et « influencer un choix à la création » (ici, changer de
   famille) touche deux mécanismes différents — celui-ci n'a pas d'équivalent
